title: Introduction
description: Software 3.0 and why it changes everything

objectives.text: Tell Software 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0 apart by how the machine's behaviour is defined in each era
Explain why working with an agent is co-thinking and not “AI does it instead of me”, and what stays with the human
Rewrite a command as a delegation and a spec: add context, the “why” and “what not to do”
Decide which part of a task to hand to the agent and which to keep for yourself
Choose which AI clone to start with, and name the steps of its build cycle

checks.question: How does Software 2.0 differ from Software 1.0?
options: In 2.0 the machine is given examples it learns from, not rules
In 2.0 code is still written by hand, just faster
In 2.0 agents execute code from our intent
In 2.0 the computer does exactly what it's told, line by line
checks.explain: In Software 1.0 a human writes the rules by hand; in 2.0 neural networks learn from data. Agents executing intent are already 3.0 (u1, “Three eras of programming”).

checks.question: What stays with the human in Software 3.0?
options: Nothing: the agent takes on both the intent and the decision
Only typing the code the agent can't write
The intent, the choice of how to work, and the final decision
Only launching the agent; after that it decides everything itself
checks.explain: The lesson says not “AI writes instead of me” but “co-thinking and co-working”. You set the intent, you work together with the agent, and the decision stays with you (u1, the “Before / Now” table).

checks.question: The AI returned something not quite what you meant. Where does the lesson advise looking for the cause first?
options: In the model: it means this tool is weak
In the “map” you gave it: which landmarks and context it lacked
In chance: just repeating the same request is enough
In yourself: it means you can't work with AI
checks.explain: The AI follows the map you gave it and invents what isn't on it. So start with what was and wasn't in the request, rather than blaming the tool or yourself (u1, reflection).

checks.question: Which request is closest to the “From commands → to delegation” shift?
options: “Write a function”
“Write a validation function, quickly”
“Do it like last time”
“I need an email validation module with error logging for a production project”
checks.explain: Delegation is explaining a task to a colleague: what is needed, what for, and in what context. “Write a function” and “quickly” remain commands without meaning (u2, shift 1).

checks.question: The agent's first answer didn't fit. How does the “From results → to experiments” shift suggest looking at this?
options: The prompt failed; better to do the task yourself
You need to switch to another tool
It's a draft and data for the next iteration
You need to send the same request again unchanged
checks.explain: The first answer is a draft, and a bad prompt is data about what to clarify. Then you iterate rather than give up (u2, shift 2).

checks.question: The prompt makes clear what to do and how, but the agent adds extra stuff every time. Which element of the spec is most likely missing?
options: “Who”
“How”
None: extra stuff is an unavoidable trait of agents
“What not to do”
checks.explain: A good spec has who / what / why / how / what not to do. Constraints are a separate part: without it the agent decides for itself where to stop (u2, shift 3 and the “Add constraints” practice).

checks.question: Which of these does the lesson advise keeping for yourself rather than delegating to the agent?
options: The final review
The first draft
Searching for information
Routine operations
checks.explain: The lesson suggests handing routine, the first draft and search to the agent. Strategy, final review and ethics stay with you (u2, shift 4).

checks.question: Which of the four shifts does the lesson call the only right one?
options: Delegation: the others are special cases of it
None: they are different ways of co-working, and each fits a different task
Specifications: without a spec the others don't work
Attention management: it's the main one
checks.explain: The four shifts are facets of co-working, not a ladder with one right rung. You choose the way to fit the task (u2, the introduction to “Four shifts in working with AI agents”; u1, “I choose the way of co-thinking that fits the task”).

checks.question: Which AI clone does the lesson advise starting with?
options: All five at once, to see the big picture
The one whose tasks cost you the most time
The one that's easiest to build technically
The one that saves the most hours according to the table, regardless of your work
checks.explain: Don't build all five at once. Pick your first clone where you yourself lose the most; the hours in the table are a guide, not a rule (u3, “Five types of AI clones”).

checks.question: The first version of the clone is built. What comes next in the build cycle?
options: Check how it works and refine it
Start building the next clone right away
Collect the source data again from scratch
Nothing: the built clone is finished
checks.explain: The cycle is Capture → Build → Test → Refine: after building, the clone is tested and refined. It's the same iterative approach as in the “From results → to experiments” shift (u3, u2).
